message:
feat(host): capture previews somewhere the host can give up on

Product 5, test 1, build 1. This is the wiring: the control session no longer calls
capture_window_thumbnail itself, and the budget from 8822c59 is finally connected to something.

On 2026-09-15 one window's preview held the host's only control dispatcher for 1h50m. Every
session on that machine failed for the duration -- connect, first pong, window list, picker, and
then fifteen seconds of nothing. The dispatcher is one per process and it was inside
PrintWindow, so it never got back to reading.

The capture now runs in GNLinkCapture, which gains a one-shot --thumbnail mode: open the
mapping, call the product's own capture_window_thumbnail, write the block, set the event, exit.
It shares --mapping with the streaming contract and nothing else, and it is checked before that
contract's required arguments so neither mode demands the other's. An older worker handed
--thumbnail does not know the flag, falls through, and exits 2 -- which the host reads as a
failed capture and skips the window, rather than waiting on events nobody will set.

A process rather than a thread, for a reason established by measurement rather than preference.
PW_RENDERFULLCONTENT is served from the DWM redirection surface on this OS -- a window that
never returns from WM_PRINT still yields a thumbnail in 24ms and its WM_PRINT counter stays at
zero. So a stuck capture is stuck inside DWM, not inside the application, and nothing in user
mode can cancel a thread that is. Ending a process is the only reclamation available.

Teardown order is not negotiable and the destructor enforces it: end the helper, WAIT for it,
and only then unmap the view it was writing into. Releasing that memory while the helper might
still be alive is the use-after-free this design exists to avoid. A job object with
KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE is the backstop, and the helper is assigned to it before it is resumed, so a
helper that escapes into the wild is not a state that exists.

The helper is not trusted about what it wrote. The host re-derives the byte count from width and
height instead of believing the header, and a block that fails any of that is Failed rather than
pixels. "No result" is always the done event not being set -- never an exit code, so a helper
that dies without exiting cleanly is the same case as one that never started.

The budget is a function-local static, which is to say per process, not per session. The
09-15 host watched three sessions in a row walk into the same window; per-session state would
have reset the count each time and paid the deadline again on every one.

One second, from the measurements in 224d25a: the most expensive window type tried costs 41.6ms
at worst, so this is about twenty five times that. Loose on purpose -- being late costs one
preview, being early costs a preview that would have arrived, and the budget is what stops a
genuinely stuck window charging a full deadline every time.

14 end-to-end checks, three clean runs, and no test hook anywhere in the product. The helper is
resolved beside the running executable, so staging a scratch directory with a chosen
GNLinkCapture.exe next to a copy of the test exercises the real CreateProcessW, the real mapping
and the real wait: with the real helper it returns pixels in 138ms; with one that sleeps for two
minutes it returns TimedOut in 549ms against a 400ms deadline, claims no pixels, and leaves
nothing running -- 737ms end to end instead of two minutes. With no helper at all it fails at
once rather than waiting.

That last case is the negative control the WM_PRINT fixture could not be. A window that ignores
WM_PRINT does not block this path at all, so the stall has to be injected where we own the
process.

Not done: a real session. Nothing here has been run against a live client, and the picker
showing a skipped window on a real host is still unproven.
